chunks: And what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:
I asked him about a well of water into which a basket of dry or wet feces had fallen, or a basket of manure. Is wudu (ablution) from it valid? He said: There is no harm in it.

The proper way to understand these two reports is one of two possibilities: one of them is that the intended meaning is that there is no harm in it after drawing out fifty buckets, in accordance with what the first report contained. The second is that what is meant by the well is a constructed reservoir in which there is more than a kurr of water; and for this reason he said there is no harm in it when there is abundant water in it, because that is where smallness and abundance are taken into consideration, unlike specified wells.

key_terms.الْقِلَّةُ وَ الْكَثْرَةُ: smallness and abundance as factors in determining the ruling
key_terms.بِئْرِ: a well from which water is drawn
key_terms.خَمْسِينَ دَلْوًا: fifty buckets to be removed from the water source
key_terms.عَذِرَةٍ: feces; impure filth falling into the water
key_terms.كُرٍّ: a large legal measure of water affecting purity rulings
key_terms.نَزْحِ: drawing out water from the well

ai.seo_question: Can wudu (ablution) be performed from a well into which feces or manure has fallen?
ai.summary: This report discusses the ruling on water in a well or reservoir when impure matter falls into it and whether wudu (ablution) may still be performed from it. The accompanying explanation reconciles the reports by either requiring the removal of fifty buckets of water or by interpreting the case as referring to a large body of water exceeding a kurr, where abundance affects the ruling.
